blocks.text: Quick Analysis is not in Excel for Mac

Quick Analysis is a Windows feature. Excel for Mac does not include it, and the answers on Microsoft's own Q&A forum say so. A thread titled Quick analysis for Excel on mac was asked in September 2015, on Excel for Mac 15.14. Its accepted answer says the feature is not available on Mac. A 2016 reply from a Microsoft MVP points readers to the Excel for Mac UserVoice forum for feature requests.

The same answer shows up again and again. In June 2022, a thread titled There is no quick analysis tool or an ideas button got a reply from MVP Jim G. He said Ideas was replaced by Analyze Data on both Mac and Windows. On 11 September 2025, MVP Bob Jones replied that the Quick Analysis button does not exist in Excel for Mac.

Some people read the big numbers on those threads as proof that Microsoft is ignoring the request. The label on the 2015 thread reads 'Same question (1600+)'. That label counts related questions, not votes. Treat it as a sign of demand, not a poll result.
No Microsoft help page we checked covers Quick Analysis on Mac. The Microsoft help page that does cover Mac is Analyze Data. Start there, and use the rest of this guide to work with it.
What to use instead: Analyze Data on the Home tab

Analyze Data is the closest built-in tool in Excel for Mac. Microsoft says it was renamed from Ideas, with the same functionality. Its help page has tabs for Windows, macOS and the web, and it applies to Excel for Microsoft 365 for Mac.

The tool looks at a table of data and shows you visuals about it in a task pane. You can insert those results as a table, a chart or a PivotTable. If your goal is a quick chart or a quick summary, start here. If you need a different job, the table below points to the guides for it.

blocks.text: Step by step: run Analyze Data on a Mac

The steps at the top of this page cover the routine. The sections below cover the edge cases that stop the tool from working. Save a copy of the workbook before you insert any results. That way you can compare the new objects with your original data.
Prepare your data before you click

Analyze Data is fussy about layout. It expects a single row of column headers, and each header should be unique and not blank. If your sheet has a title across the top, two header rows or a merged cell in the header, move the data or fix the headers first. Otherwise the results will be hard to trust.

Dates need care too. Microsoft notes that text dates such as 2017-01-01 are treated as text. If a date column is left-aligned, it is probably text. Convert the column to real dates before you run the analysis, so the tool can group and sort them.

Save the file as .xlsx, .xlsm or .xlsb. The feature does not work on .xls files in compatibility mode. If you opened an old workbook, use File > Save As and pick a modern format. Then reopen the file and try again.
Size limits and how to work around them

Analyze Data does not support datasets over 1.5 million cells. Microsoft's workaround is to filter the data and copy the filtered rows to another sheet or workbook. Run the analysis there. Cells count rows times columns, including the header row.
A wide sheet hits the limit sooner than a narrow one. Check the width as well as the length. A sheet with many columns and a long history of rows is the most common reason people hit the wall.
Worked example: a sheet of orders

Say you have a sheet with one row per order. The columns are Order date, Region, Product, Units and Amount. The header row sits in row 1, and every header has a name. Click any cell inside the block, then press ⌘T so Excel treats the range as a table. That step is optional, but it keeps the headers and range tied together as you add rows.

Now choose Home > Analyze Data. The pane shows visuals about the orders. If one of them answers your question, insert it. You can keep it as a chart, a PivotTable or a table. If none of them fits, close the pane and build the view you need by hand.

Check the result before you share it. Pick two or three rows from the source and add them up yourself. If your total matches the inserted object, the analysis is probably right. If it does not, check the header names and the range again.
When Analyze Data is missing from the Home tab

Some Mac users report that the button disappears. One user saw the Analyze Data button next to Find & Select in version 16.49. After updating to 16.63, it was gone. A moderator could not reproduce the problem on 16.63.

Start with Help > Check for Updates. Then open Excel > Preferences > Ribbon and Toolbar. MVP Jim G suggested this route to bring the button back. Make sure Analyze Data is enabled in that list, then return to the Home tab.

The latest build we found is 16.114.3, Build 26102720, dated October 27, 2026. The release notes for that build and the two before it do not mention Analyze Data. An update alone may not change anything, so check the Ribbon settings if the button is still missing.
Limits, languages and the Ideas name

Natural-language questions are rolling out gradually. Microsoft says they may not be available in every country or region. The supported languages listed are English, French, Spanish, German, Simplified Chinese and Japanese. If your language is not on that list, do not count on typed questions.

Ideas and Analyze Data are the same feature under two names. Microsoft says some users on the Semi-Annual Enterprise Channel may still see Ideas until Excel is updated. If your menu says Ideas, update Excel before you go looking for a different tool.

Analyze Data is not Quick Analysis. Do not expect a pop-up action button to appear when you select a range. That behavior is part of Quick Analysis on Windows. The MVP replies say it does not exist on Mac.
Keyboard shortcuts and the Ctrl+Q myth

You will find sites that say Ctrl+Q opens Quick Analysis. That shortcut is for Windows, and the claim comes from third-party tutorials, not from Microsoft. Some of those sites also say Command+Q works on Mac. The Microsoft Q&A replies contradict that, so do not rely on it. If you want to test it, use a copy of the workbook.
The shortcut you can trust here is ⌘T. Microsoft's Analyze Data page lists Command+T as the Mac shortcut for creating a table. The same page lists Ctrl+T for Windows.
The MVP answering in 2025 says you can assign a keyboard shortcut to Analyze Data. The thread does not give the exact menu path. Check Excel's Help for the current steps before you rely on one.
Mistakes people make with Analyze Data

items: Starting with a title row above the headers, so the tool reads the title as a column name.
Pasting dates from a web page or an export, which often brings in text dates.
Saving in .xls compatibility mode, where the feature does not work.
Selecting only part of the data, then wondering why the visuals leave out rows.
Running the tool on a sheet over 1.5 million cells without filtering first.
Expecting the same pop-up behavior as Quick Analysis on Windows.

blocks.text: Other Mac tools for similar work

If Analyze Data does not give you what you need, use one of the guides below. Each one shows steps for Microsoft 365. Start with the [pivot table guide](/how-to/make-a-pivot-table-in-excel) if you want to group rows. Use the [sparkline guide](/how-to/insert-a-sparkline-in-excel) for a small chart inside one cell. The [trendline guide](/how-to/add-a-trendline-to-a-chart-in-excel) covers charts that need a trend line.
Send Microsoft feedback about Quick Analysis

If you still want Quick Analysis on Mac, say so to Microsoft. A 2022 MVP reply suggests Help > Feedback > I Have a Suggestion. A 2016 reply points to the Excel for Mac UserVoice forum. We did not open that forum, so we cannot confirm it is still active.
What to try next

Open a sheet you already know well, so you can judge whether the visuals are right. Give it a clean header row, click a cell, and press ⌘T. Then run Home > Analyze Data and compare the result with a number you can check by hand. Once that works, try the same steps on a larger sheet.

faq.question: Is Quick Analysis available in Excel for Mac?
faq.answer: No. Microsoft Q&A replies from MVPs, dated from 2016 to 2025, say the feature is not in Excel for Mac. The closest option is Analyze Data on the Home tab.

faq.question: Where is Analyze Data in Excel on Mac?
faq.answer: It is on the Home tab. Click any cell in your data range first, then choose Home > Analyze Data. A task pane opens with visuals about your data.

faq.question: What is the Quick Analysis shortcut on Mac?
faq.answer: There is no confirmed Mac shortcut for Quick Analysis. Ctrl+Q is the Windows shortcut. Claims that Command+Q works on Mac come from third-party sites, and they conflict with the MVP replies. Use ⌘T to create a table.

faq.question: Why did Analyze Data disappear after an update?
faq.answer: One user saw it vanish after moving from version 16.49 to 16.63. Check for updates with Help > Check for Updates, then enable the button in Excel > Preferences > Ribbon and Toolbar. A moderator could not reproduce the problem on 16.63.

faq.question: How big can my data be for Analyze Data?
faq.answer: Microsoft says the feature does not support datasets over 1.5 million cells. For larger data, filter the rows you need, copy them to a new sheet or workbook, and run the analysis there.

faq.question: Does Analyze Data work in .xls files?
faq.answer: Not in compatibility mode. Save the file as .xlsx, .xlsm or .xlsb, then reopen it and try again.

faq.question: Is Analyze Data the same as Ideas in Excel?
faq.answer: Microsoft says Ideas was renamed Analyze Data, with the same functionality. Some users on the Semi-Annual Enterprise Channel may still see Ideas until Excel is updated.

faq.question: Can I ask Analyze Data questions in plain English?
faq.answer: Microsoft says natural-language queries are rolling out gradually, and they may not be available in every country or region. Listed languages are English, French, Spanish, German, Simplified Chinese and Japanese.

task: Use Analyze Data in Excel on Mac
appliesTo: Excel for Microsoft 365 for Mac, current builds
requirements: A data range with one header row
Analyze Data enabled on the Home tab

steps.name: Check for updates first
steps.text: Open Help > Check for Updates and install what Microsoft offers. The Analyze Data button was reported missing after an update on version 16.63, so start with a current build.
steps.tip: The latest build in the release notes we checked is 16.114.3, dated October 27, 2026.

steps.name: Make sure the data has one header row
steps.text: Look at the top row of your range. Each column needs a unique, non-blank header, and the headers must sit in a single row. Remove titles or merged cells above the headers.

steps.name: Format the range as a table
steps.text: Click any cell in the data, then press Command+T. This turns the range into a table. Microsoft lists Command+T as the Mac shortcut for creating a table.

steps.name: Click a cell inside the data range
steps.text: Select any cell inside the range you want to analyze. Analyze Data works from the range around that cell. Do not pick an empty cell outside the block.

steps.name: Open Analyze Data
steps.text: Click the Home tab, then click Analyze Data. A task pane opens with visuals about your data.
steps.tip: If the button is missing, see the troubleshooting section below.

steps.name: Read the suggested visuals
steps.text: Look through the visuals in the pane. Each one summarizes the data. Check the column names and the totals before you trust a suggestion.

steps.name: Insert the result you want
steps.text: Choose the visual you need and insert it as a table, a chart or a PivotTable. Microsoft lists these three result types.

steps.name: Ask a question in plain language
steps.text: If your region and language are supported, the pane may let you type a question about the data. Microsoft says this is rolling out gradually, so you may not see it yet.
steps.tip: Listed languages are English, French, Spanish, German, Simplified Chinese and Japanese.

shortcuts.action: Create a table from the selected range

troubleshooting.problem: Analyze Data is missing from the Home tab
troubleshooting.fix: Update Excel with Help > Check for Updates. Then open Excel > Preferences > Ribbon and Toolbar and make sure Analyze Data is enabled. One user reported it disappearing on version 16.63, and a moderator could not reproduce it.

troubleshooting.problem: The tool says the data is too large
troubleshooting.fix: Microsoft's limit is 1.5 million cells. Filter the rows you need, copy them to a new sheet or workbook, and run Analyze Data there.
Text dates such as 2017-01-01 are treated as text. Convert the column to real dates, then run the tool again. A left-aligned date column is a quick sign of text.

troubleshooting.problem: Analyze Data does not work in an older file
troubleshooting.fix: Files in .xls compatibility mode are not supported. Use File > Save As, choose .xlsx, .xlsm or .xlsb, then reopen the file.

troubleshooting.problem: The Quick Analysis shortcut does nothing
troubleshooting.fix: Ctrl+Q is a Windows shortcut, and Command+Q claims come from third-party sites that conflict with Microsoft Q&A replies. Use Home > Analyze Data instead.
